title: Where are reports in Google Analytics 4 left navigation on Mac, and how to add them
metaTitle: Where are reports in Google Analytics 4 left navigation on Mac
description: GA4 shows standard reports in the left navigation only through Library collections. Here is how to find them, add them, and fix what blocks you.

intro: Standard reports in Google Analytics 4 reach the left navigation only through Library report collections. Click Library at the bottom of the left navigation, add the report to a collection, and publish that collection. This page shows where reports live, how to add one step by step, why one goes missing, and the limits you will hit.
tldr: Standard GA4 reports reach the left navigation only through Library report collections.
Only Administrators and Editors see Library and can change collections. Viewers do not.
A collection must be published before its reports appear. Unpublishing removes them.
Google's limits: 7 collections per property, 5 topics per collection, 10 reports per topic.
Collections sort alphabetically and cannot be reordered, so plan your names.

blocks.text: Where are reports in Google Analytics 4 left navigation

Standard reports in GA4 reach the left navigation only through Library report collections. Reports sit in the Reports section, but that does not mean they show on the left. You add them to a collection, publish it, and then they appear.

So when you ask where the reports are, you are really asking two things. First, where the report lives. Second, whether it sits in a published collection that the left navigation shows. If a report is missing from the left side, it is probably still in the Reports section. It just never went into a collection.
Check three places, in this order, before you assume a report is gone.

items: The Reports section. This is where standard and custom reports live.
Library, at the bottom of the left navigation. Only Administrators and Editors see it.
The collection card inside Library. Check that it is published before you decide the report is gone.

blocks.text: Library is the middle layer. Think of three levels: a collection, topics inside it, and reports inside each topic. A collection can hold up to five topics. A topic can hold up to ten reports. The left navigation shows what sits inside the published collections, in that same structure.
How to add a report to the left navigation in GA4

items: Click Library at the bottom of the left navigation.
Find the report you want in the Reports section. If it is not there, create it first.
Put the report in a collection. Choose an existing collection or make a new one.
Make sure the collection is published. On its card, click More, then click Publish.
Drag the report into a topic inside that collection.
Look at the left navigation and confirm the collection and the report now show.

blocks.text: Here is an example. Say your team checks acquisition numbers every Monday. Make a collection called Weekly checks. Put the acquisition report in a topic inside it. Publish the collection, then open the left navigation and confirm the report is there before your Monday review starts.
Why you cannot see Library at the bottom of the nav

Library shows only for people with the Administrator or Editor role. Viewers do not see it, and they cannot change collections. If Library is missing from your screen, that is an access question, not a broken menu. Ask an Administrator or Editor for the change. Spending more time looking will not change your role.
Why a report is missing from the left navigation
Work through the causes in order. The first two are the quickest to check, and they cover the most common cases you will see on a normal day. Check the table before you rebuild anything.

rows: No Library option at the bottom of the nav
Ask an Administrator or Editor to make the change or add the report
The collection exists, but its reports do not show
Open Library, click More on the collection card, then click Publish
Reuse a collection you already have
A report will not fit in a topic
Start a new topic, or use a different collection
Collections are in an order you did not choose
Choose collection names that sort the way you want
blocks.caption: Common causes, checked in order

blocks.text: The table covers the usual blockers. It does not cover a report you never saved, or a collection you can see but cannot edit. For those, check the Save step first. Then ask an admin to confirm your access on the property.
GA4 report collection limits: 7 collections, 5 topics, 10 reports

Google's help page sets three hard limits. Each property can have up to 7 report collections. A collection can have up to 5 topics. A topic can have up to 10 reports, and only one of them can be an overview report.
Teams often make one collection per person or per question. That uses up the seven slots fast. Plan around the collection count first, because it is the easiest limit to hit and the hardest to undo.

Keep one collection for each recurring review, such as weekly checks or the monthly report for leadership. Leave out reports nobody opens. A short, well-named set beats a crowded menu that no one reads.
Why GA4 collections sort alphabetically

Google's help page says collections appear in the left navigation in alphabetical order by collection name. You cannot reorder them. Topics and reports inside a collection can be reordered by dragging.

Some third-party guides say numbering the collection names controls the order. I could not confirm that on Google's page. Test it in your own property before you rename a collection that people already use.
What Universal Analytics changes mean for your reports

Universal Analytics standard properties stopped processing data on July 1, 2023. Access to UA data ended in the week of July 1, 2024. Many teams rebuilt their reports in GA4 from scratch. Each new report then needed its own place in a collection, which can explain why a new GA4 left navigation looks thin.

Google's migration Q&A says you cannot move historical UA data into GA4. GA4 holds only data collected since the GA4 property was set up. Google lists CSV, Excel, Google Sheets, PDF, and other export routes for UA reports. Those routes needed to happen before UA access ended.
What missing reports cost you in time and trust

I could not find a study that measures the minutes lost to finding or adding GA4 reports. Treat any number for this exact task with suspicion. The figures below come from general workplace research, so they show a pattern, not your cost.

Asana's Anatomy of Work Index, based on more than 10,000 knowledge workers, says 60% of time at work goes to work about work. That category includes searching for information. A 2019 B2B Marketing article, citing a Kingpin study, says marketing reports and analysis take 32% of working hours. Neither source measures GA4.

Measure your own cost. For one week, write down each time you look for a report and how long it takes. Multiply those minutes by how often you search, then by the number of weeks you care about. That number beats any general figure.
Trust is the other cost. When people cannot find a report, they ask a colleague or rebuild it. Then two versions of the same report circulate, and nobody knows which one is current.
Ask an admin for access in one message
Ask for the role you need in one message. Name the property, the report, and the change. Specific requests are easier to act on than a vague note that says the menu is broken.

Here is a draft you can edit and send from your own account. Lazur can draft it too, but you send it. 'Hi [name], could you give me Editor access on the [property name] GA4 property? I want to add the [report name] report to a collection in the left navigation. Thanks.'
If you only read reports, Viewer access may be enough. You need Editor access to add reports to the left navigation, so ask for that only if you will add them.
Regulated data and shared reports

Many GA4 properties hold data about customers, patients, or clients. If your job is regulated, such as in law, nursing, or accounting, follow your employer's rules for that data. Do that before you share a report or a screenshot. Ask your data owner or compliance contact first.
Mistakes people make with GA4 report navigation

items: Adding a report to a collection, then forgetting to publish the collection.
Making a new collection for every question, then hitting the limit of seven.
Assuming a missing report was deleted. It is often unpublished or outside a topic.
Reading Library as broken when the account has Viewer access.
Following an old screenshot. Google says its labels may change, and the help page shows no update date.

blocks.text: Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur helps most with the part you cannot see on your own. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask where Library is. Lazur sees your screen, draws a circle and a label around Library, and answers out loud. Then ask for a walkthrough. It guides you one click at a time and waits for each click.

Lazur does not click for you. It cannot change your role in GA4, and it cannot publish a collection for you. It can draft the access message, explain why a collection is not showing, and run background research in its own Chrome tabs. Google changes labels, so trust the screen over any guide, Lazur included.
After the report shows up in the left navigation

Open the report from the left navigation once, using the date range you use in your weekly review. Check that the numbers look right. If they do not, check the property and the date range before you blame the menu.
Then write down the collection name and the topic where the report sits. Put that note in a shared Google Doc. The next person who asks where the report is gets an answer in a minute.

faq.question: Where are reports in Google Analytics 4 left navigation?
faq.answer: Standard reports reach the left navigation through Library, at the bottom of the left navigation. Add the report to a collection, publish the collection, and it shows on the left. Reports you have not added may still exist in the Reports section.

faq.question: Why can't I see Library in GA4?
faq.answer: Library shows only for the Administrator and Editor roles. Viewer access hides it. Ask an Administrator to check your role on the property, or ask them to add the report for you.

faq.question: Why did my report disappear from the left navigation?
faq.answer: Check whether its collection is still published. Google says unpublishing a collection removes its reports from the left navigation. The report may still exist in Library or in the Reports section.

faq.question: How many reports can I add to the GA4 left navigation?
faq.answer: Google's help page sets 7 collections per property, 5 topics per collection, and 10 reports per topic. A topic can have only one overview report.

faq.question: Can I reorder collections in the GA4 left navigation?
faq.answer: Google's help page says collections appear alphabetically and cannot be reordered. You can drag topics and reports inside a collection. Some guides suggest numbering names, but I did not confirm that, so test it first.

faq.question: Can I move historical Universal Analytics data into GA4?
faq.answer: No. Google's migration Q&A says historical UA data cannot be migrated into GA4. GA4 holds only data collected since the property was set up. UA data had to be exported before UA access ended.

faq.question: Does this work on a Mac?
faq.answer: GA4 runs in a web browser. Google's help page does not name a browser or platform, and I did not verify browser-specific behavior. These steps assume Chrome on a Mac, so check your own screen against them.

faq.question: Can Lazur add the report for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur points at things, guides you one click at a time, and waits for each click. It does not click buttons or operate other apps for you.

costs.title: Minutes lost on every search
costs.text: Each time you hunt for a report, you pay in minutes. I found no study that measures that for GA4 navigation, so the number is yours to measure. Count the searches for one week and the minutes each one takes. That count is the honest starting point.

costs.title: Waiting on admin access
costs.text: Viewers cannot add a report until an Administrator or Editor acts. The request can sit in an inbox until someone answers. Plan for that wait before a deadline depends on the report.

costs.title: Reports you stop opening
costs.text: A report you cannot find is a report you may stop opening. Then the decision it was meant to inform gets made without it. That cost is quiet, so it rarely shows up on a time sheet.

costs.title: Duplicate reports and conflicting numbers
costs.text: When people cannot find a report, they rebuild it. Two versions of one report can show different numbers. Nobody knows which one to trust in a meeting, and the argument starts there.

causes.title: Library is the only path into the left navigation
causes.text: Standard reports do not appear in the left navigation on their own. Google's help page says they reach it only through Library report collections. A report you have not added to a collection stays out of sight, even if it sits in the Reports section.

causes.title: Only Administrators and Editors can change collections
causes.text: Library and collection changes are limited to two roles. A Viewer can read reports but cannot add them to the navigation. Many people do not know their role until they go looking for Library.

causes.title: Unpublished collections stay hidden
causes.text: A saved collection is not enough. It must be published before its reports show. Google says unpublishing removes its reports from the left navigation. A collection you saved but never published looks finished, and it still does not show.

causes.title: Hard limits on collections, topics, and reports
causes.text: Each property can have 7 collections. Each collection holds up to 5 topics, and each topic holds up to 10 reports. Once you hit a limit, the next report has nowhere to go, so you must reuse or reorganize.

causes.title: Alphabetical collection order
causes.text: Collections appear alphabetically by name, and you cannot drag them into another order. A name that sorts late can look buried, even when it matters most. Choose names with that order in mind.

causes.title: Reports rebuilt after the Universal Analytics sunset
causes.text: Universal Analytics stopped processing data on July 1, 2023. Many teams made new GA4 reports from scratch, and each one needed its own place in a collection. Many of those reports were never placed there, so the navigation looks thin.

causes.title: Interface labels and guides change
causes.text: The Google help page I checked shows no publication or last-updated date. Third-party guides can be out of date. Menu names may move, so check the live screen before you follow an old screenshot.

fixes.title: Check your role first
fixes.text: Look at the bottom of the left navigation for Library. If it is missing, you probably have Viewer access. Ask an Administrator or Editor to make the change or add the report for you. That message is faster than searching for a menu your role does not show.

fixes.title: Publish the collection before you check
fixes.text: Open Library, find the collection card, click More, then click Publish. Google says a collection must be published before its reports appear in the left navigation. Then refresh the page and look at the left navigation again.

fixes.title: Follow the save sequence in order
fixes.text: Add the report to a collection, publish the collection, click Edit collection, drag the report into a topic, and click Save. Google's sequence ends with Save. Skipping that last step can leave the report somewhere you did not expect.

fixes.title: Keep collections few and purposeful
fixes.text: Plan seven collections at most, grouped by the job they serve, such as weekly checks, campaign reviews, and monthly reporting. Reuse a collection before you create a new one. Keep each collection to five topics and each topic to ten reports.

fixes.title: Name collections for alphabetical order
fixes.text: Google says collections sort alphabetically and cannot be reordered. If order matters, choose names that sort the way your team reads them. Test the order in your own property before you rename anything that people already use.

fixes.title: Drag topics and reports into the order you want
fixes.text: Google says topics and reports inside a collection can be reordered by dragging. Put the report you open most near the top of its topic. A small change like this saves scrolling every week.

fixes.title: Keep one shared list of report locations
fixes.text: Make a Google Doc with four columns: report name, collection, topic, and date added. Update it when you add a report. The list answers the where is this question without a new search.

fixes.title: Check what you still need from Universal Analytics
fixes.text: Google says UA data had to be exported to be kept after access ended, and access ended in the week of July 1, 2024. Look through old exports and files. If you find a useful UA export, copy the figures you need into Google Sheets so they stay with your team.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Check your role and Library access
plan.text: Open GA4 and look at the bottom of the left navigation. If Library is missing, your role is probably Viewer. Write that down, then send the access request from the draft in this guide.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: List the reports you open each week
plan.text: Write down the five reports you open most. For each one, note whether it already shows in the left navigation. Find the ones that do not show in the Reports section.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Plan your collections on paper
plan.text: Plan no more than seven collections. Group reports by the job they serve, such as weekly checks or monthly reviews. Keep each collection to five topics and each topic to ten reports.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Build and publish one collection
plan.text: Follow the eight steps in this guide for one collection only. Publish it, refresh the page, and confirm the reports show in the left navigation. Fix any gaps before you start the next one.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Finish the rest and write the log
plan.text: Add the remaining reports, then update your shared Google Doc. Each row should hold the report name, collection, topic, and date added. Share the doc with the team that uses those reports.
